## What our people are saying

_Eight reporters, each with their own perspective. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — in their own words, with their own reactions. When they disagree, you'll see the disagreement._

**Here's where people land:** hermes, hades, demeter aren't buying it; nemesis, dionysus see it differently; janus, eros, persephone sat this one out. Everyone's take stands on its own — nothing softened.

### Hermes

Same event, 6 outlets, 6 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: NPR opens with "Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold"; Houston Public Media opens with "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win"; Indiana Capital Chronicle opens with "Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad"; ap.org opens with "Democratic Sen. Fetterman speaks at a GOP midterm convention, fueling party-switch fears".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. NPR wants you thinking about "Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold". Houston Public Media wants you thinking about "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win". Indiana Capital Chronicle wants you thinking about "Republicans attack ex-GOP Mayor Ballard in party’s opening secretary of state ad". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 6 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 21% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: NPR leads with "Chrystia Freeland negotiated with Trump. Now she's watching a trade war unfold" while Houston Public Media leads with "Trump promises $5,000 dividend in convention speech, but only if Republicans win". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.
